The most convenient way to understand linear operators is in terms of their matrix representations.
In fact, the linear operator and matrix viewpoints turn out to be completely equivalent.
The matrix viewpoint may be more familiar to you, however.
To see the connection, it helps to first understand that an $m$ by $n$ complex matrix $A$ with entries $A_{i j}$ is in fact a linear operator sending vectors in the vector space $\mathbf{C}^{n}$ to the vector space $\mathbf{C}^{m}$, under matrix multiplication of the matrix $A$ by a vector in $\mathbf{C}^{n}$.
More precisely, the claim that the matrix $A$ is a linear operator just means that

$$
\begin{equation*}
A\left(\sum_{i} a_{i}\left|v_{i}\right\rangle\right)=\sum_{i} a_{i} A\left|v_{i}\right\rangle \tag{2.11}
\end{equation*}
$$

is true as an equation where the operation is matrix multiplication of $A$ by column vectors.
Clearly, this is true!

We've seen that matrices can be regarded as linear operators.
Can linear operators be given a matrix representation?
In fact they can, as we now explain.
This equivalence between the two viewpoints justifies our interchanging terms from matrix theory and operator theory throughout the book.
Suppose $A: V \rightarrow W$ is a linear operator between vector spaces $V$ and $W$.
Suppose $\left|v_{1}\right\rangle, \ldots,\left|v_{m}\right\rangle$ is a basis for $V$ and $\left|w_{1}\right\rangle, \ldots,\left|w_{n}\right\rangle$ is a basis for $W$.
Then for each $j$ in the range $1, \ldots, m$, there exist complex numbers $A_{1 j}$ through $A_{n j}$ such that

$$
\begin{equation*}
A\left|v_{j}\right\rangle=\sum_{i} A_{i j}\left|w_{i}\right\rangle \tag{2.12}
\end{equation*}
$$

The matrix whose entries are the values $A_{i j}$ is said to form a matrix representation of the operator $A$.
This matrix representation of $A$ is completely equivalent to the operator $A$, and we will use the matrix representation and abstract operator viewpoints interchangeably.
Note that to make the connection between matrices and linear operators we must specify a set of input and output basis states for the input and output vector spaces of the linear operator.
<<<END_ITEM>>>
